transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-28
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Park (Redwood SE), Aisha Rahman (Redwood SE), Rosa Martinez (Sentinel), Jonah Lee (Sentinel), Priya Nair (Sentinel), Samir O'Connor (Sentinel)

Summary:
Quick POC scoping to nail down success criteria, reserved GPU sizing, burst strategy and fallback policies. Agree on benchmark window, what metrics we'll collect (latency p50/p95, cost per 1k requests, throughput), and security check-ins.

Topics: success criteria; workload sizing; benchmark plan; reserved vs burst capacity; graceful fallbacks; timelines and deliverables.

Action items (captured in metadata above).

Transcript:
00:00 Maya (Redwood AE): All right everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro — I'm Maya, AE on the account, and Daniel and Aisha from SE will handle the tech. Can we do quick round robin?
00:12 Rosa (Sentinel): Hi yeah Rosa here, Head of Platform. Jonah is ML infra and Priya is CTO, Samir is SRE. We're really trying to validate cost + latency before committing to a reserved pool.
00:25 Daniel (Redwood SE): Great. High level agenda — align on SLOs, capture a sample workload, propose reserved GPU quantity for the 4-week POC, define burst strategy and fallback behavior, then agree benchmark dates.
00:32 Jonah (Sentinel): Quick context — we have a production-ish traffic spike pattern. Baseline is 200 QPS during day, spiking to 800 QPS for 3–6 minute bursts, roughly 4 times an hour. Latency target is p95 under 600ms for our top-10 prompts. Cost sensitivity is high, we'd rather burst than commit too many reserved GPUs.
01:05 Aisha (Redwood SE): Okay that's helpful. When you say 200 baseline — is that user-facing text generation or embedding-ish throughput?
01:20 Jonah (Sentinel): Mostly generation; a mix of short chat replies and longer code synthesis tasks. Average token output per call is around 120 tokens, but the heavy ones go up to 800 tokens.
01:42 Priya (Sentinel): Our success criteria for the POC are threefold: 1) confirm p95 < 600ms for top prompts at expected load, 2) show predictable unit cost — i.e., cost per 1k tokens within 20% of Redwood's estimate, 3) a documented fallback that keeps user experience acceptable when the reserved pool is exhausted.
02:10 Daniel (Redwood SE): Good. For the reserved capacity suggestion we usually size for 60–80% of expected steady baseline to save cost, then rely on burst capacity for spikes. For your numbers I'd propose reserving enough to handle 150 QPS baseline with an autoscale buffer to burst to 800 using queued requests and pre-warmed instances.
02:45 Samir (Sentinel): Can you explain the burst mechanism again? We need deterministic fallbacks — we can't just drop requests.
03:00 Aisha (Redwood SE): Sure. Our recommended approach is a three-tier policy: primary reserved pool (pinned GPUs), short-term burst (warm replicas from burst pool that spin up within X seconds), and graceful fallback which can be either a lighter model variant or queued response with progress updates to the client. We also support KV cache prefixing to cut latency for repeated prefixes.
03:28 Rosa (Sentinel): When you say 'lighter model variant' — can you give an example? We don't want hallucination regressions.
03:40 Daniel (Redwood SE): Example: model-a-1.2 (float32) is your standard; model-a-quant (8-bit) is the fallback for cost/latency. We run evals on key prompts to ensure quality delta is acceptable; Redwood Optimize will surface regressions. But small accuracy deltas are expected; we can gate fallback on a confidence threshold.
04:05 Jonah (Sentinel): Who owns the gating logic — our app or Redwood? We prefer Redwood to handle automatic fallback so we don't ship brittle client code.
04:18 Maya (Redwood AE): We can manage the routing at the platform layer: policy driven. You set SLOs and fallback preferences (prioritize latency vs quality), and the runtime will route requests accordingly. We'll show the A/B style routing in the pilot.
04:36 Priya (Sentinel): Security question — how do you handle keys, logs, and data residency? Our security team will need SOC2 evidence and KMS integration.
04:50 Maya (Redwood AE): Redwood Private has customer-managed KMS options and audit logs; for hosted POC we can enable envelope encryption and restrict retention to X days. We'll share the SOC2 summary and the security addendum. Note — for a private VPC pilot it's a separate process but doable.
05:12 Rosa (Sentinel): Great. Back to sizing: can you translate reserved GPU count into expected QPS for our model shapes?
05:26 Daniel (Redwood SE): Rough numbers — on an A100-like slot, for your model (approx 7B-ish mixed workloads) you should expect about 80–120 small-generation QPS if the seq lengths are low. For your average token lengths (120 tokens) and mixed heavy calls, estimate ~30–40 QPS per GPU. So for a 150 QPS baseline you'd want about 4 reserved GPUs. This is a ballpark; benchmarks will confirm.
06:05 Jonah (Sentinel): 4 reserved GPUs to serve baseline, and then burst up to what?
06:12 Aisha (Redwood SE): Burst pool can be cold or warm VMs that spin up additional GPUs — practically we can allow bursts up to 12 GPUs but spin-up time varies; warm burst reduces spin-up to ~15–30s. We also do request-level queuing to avoid thundering herd.
06:40 Samir (Sentinel): If spin-up is 15–30s, our spikes are 3–6 minutes — acceptable — but we need to ensure the first X seconds don't degrade UX. What's the UX during spin-up?
06:55 Daniel (Redwood SE): Options: a) short queuing (client sees spinner with ETA), b) immediate downgrade to a light model, c) partial response streaming while we warm extra capacity. For customer-facing chat we often do (b) then backfill a higher-quality completion asynchronously if requested.
07:25 Priya (Sentinel): Backfill sounds risky for product consistency. Could we test approach B with a quality gate — only downgrade when confidence drops below 0.8?
07:40 Aisha (Redwood SE): Yes, we can wire that in the POC routing policy. We'll need your eval set and acceptable thresholds.
07:52 Rosa (Sentinel): About benchmarks — what datasets do you use? We have a set of 250 critical prompts (mix of short replies and long synth tasks). Will that be sufficient?
08:05 Daniel (Redwood SE): Perfect. Send that as CSV with expected output lengths and priority flags. We'll run three bench types: steady baseline run, spike-run simulation (pattern you described), and a durability run to check memory/KV cache behavior across long sessions.
08:28 Jonah (Sentinel): Can you also capture per-token cost and S3 egress? Our infra costs matter.
08:35 Maya (Redwood AE): We'll include a tokenized cost breakdown and a per-hour reserved GPU cost. We'll show blended cost with burst usage so you can compare reserved+burst vs pure on-demand.
08:50 Priya (Sentinel): Timeline? When can we start and how long will the POC be?
09:00 Maya (Redwood AE): Proposed timeline: Week 1 (2027-01-04): exchange artifacts and sign POC terms. Week 2 (2027-01-11): staging/bench harness ready; run initial steady-state tests. Week 3 (2027-01-18): execute spike window and fallback tests. Week 4 (2027-01-25): results review and decision. So a 3–4 week cycle.
09:28 Rosa (Sentinel): That aligns with our Q1 planning. We'll need to brief procurement on estimated reserved commitment if we will go ahead.
09:40 Maya (Redwood AE): We'll include a few commitment options: 1-month reserved, 3-month with discount, or pay-as-you-go with higher per-unit cost.
09:55 Samir (Sentinel): For the reserved pool, are we locked to specific GPU types? We prefer flexibility over vendor-specific SKUs for pricing.
10:05 Aisha (Redwood SE): We map to performance-equivalent tiers. For private/on-prem it's your hardware. For hosted we offer specific instance families but can map to an equivalent SKU and guarantee throughput per model.
10:20 Jonah (Sentinel): Benchmarks — how reproducible are they? We need scripts we can run in our CI.
10:30 Daniel (Redwood SE): We'll provide the harness (python microservice + load generator) with config knobs: request mix, token lengths, concurrency. You can run it locally or against our staging endpoints. We'll also publish the exact seed prompts and randomization settings to make runs deterministic.
10:58 Priya (Sentinel): A few nitty details — does Redwood's runtime support KV cache prefetching per session? We rely on session caching to keep p95 low for multi-turn flows.
11:12 Daniel (Redwood SE): Yes, KV cache per session is supported. There's also prefix caching for repeated opening prompts which should cut token compute by up to ~30% for repetitive sequences. We'll measure that in the durability run.
11:30 Rosa (Sentinel): Ok. On fallback policies, one of our constraints: legal requires auditability — any fallback must be logged with model variant used and a reason code.
11:44 Maya (Redwood AE): We log routing metadata (model, variant, fallback_reason, latency). That gets to the audit logs and can be forwarded to your SIEM. We'll include an example schema in the doc pack.
11:58 Samir (Sentinel): Encryption at rest and transit?
12:03 Maya (Redwood AE): TLS in transit, and at-rest encryption using envelope keys. For hosted we manage keys by default; for Private we can integrate with your KMS/HSM.
12:15 Rosa (Sentinel): Great. Any blockers on our side to start?
12:22 Jonah (Sentinel): We'll need to carve out a staging VPC and provide credentials for a small service account. Also legal wants to see PII handling in the POC.
12:35 Maya (Redwood AE): We'll send a POC security checklist. You can mark PII as redacted in test dataset or we can use synthetic data.
12:45 Priya (Sentinel): On metrics, we want token-level cost, per-request latency, GPU utilization, queue length, number of fallback events, and quality delta for fallback.
12:55 Aisha (Redwood SE): All capturable. We'll instrument the harness to push metrics to your Prometheus endpoint and to our console for correlation.
13:10 Jonah (Sentinel): One more — fallback rollback. If fallback results in large quality regression we need an automatic rollback to on-prem older model. Is that supported?
13:22 Daniel (Redwood SE): We support auto-fallback but rollback to an external on-prem model requires integration — we can implement a hybrid routing rule: if fallback_quality_metric < threshold, route to your on-prem endpoint. That will be part of the integration work and we can scope it for the POC.
13:48 Rosa (Sentinel): Costs on demo? We need simple numbers to show procurement.
13:55 Maya (Redwood AE): We'll send three sample scenarios with cost per 100k tokens and monthlyized reserved cost for 4 GPUs vs 8 GPUs.
14:08 Priya (Sentinel): Let's talk about telemetry — can we get per-request traces?
14:16 Aisha (Redwood SE): Yes, we support tracing hooks and can emit OpenTelemetry spans. We'll include an example tracing snippet.
14:30 Jonah (Sentinel): Ok, I'm comfortable with the plan. A few clarifying points about the workload: some requests are latency-sensitive (p95 target), some are best-effort. We should be able to annotate priority in the request token so routing respects it.
14:48 Daniel (Redwood SE): Absolutely, request-level priority is supported — high-priority routes to reserved and low-priority uses burst or queued pool. We'll need your priority mapping in the prompt set.
15:05 Maya (Redwood AE): Quick recap then: Redwood will propose a 4 GPU reserved baseline (ballpark) + warm burst to 12 GPUs; runbench harness during week of 1/11; collect p50/p95, cost, GPU util, fallback events; wire policy gating on confidence thresholds. Action items: Maya to send pricing and security docs; Daniel to deliver harness; customer to send prompts and traffic histograms. Anything else?
15:35 Rosa (Sentinel): Also need the audit log schema and retention options.
15:42 Maya (Redwood AE): Noted. We'll add that to the doc pack.
15:50 Priya (Sentinel): And procurement will need the reserved commitment options.
15:55 Maya (Redwood AE): We'll include 1/3/6 month options and expected discounts.
16:05 Samir (Sentinel): One operational note — idle GPU eviction policies. If we reserve GPUs but want to throttle them during nights, do you support schedule-based scaling?
16:16 Aisha (Redwood SE): Yes, schedule-based scale-down and predictive autoscaling are both supported. You can define time windows and min-capacity.
16:30 Jonah (Sentinel): Great. Anything else from Redwood?
16:35 Daniel (Redwood SE): We'll also include a small stress test to validate KV cache integrity across multi-turn sessions, and a load pattern to simulate token-heavy calls.
16:47 Maya (Redwood AE): OK thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the doc pack and scheduling invite for the benchmark window.
16:55 Rosa (Sentinel): Thanks — talk soon.
17:00 [call ends] 

Notes about transcription: occasional mis-hearings: 'KV cache' sometimes transcribed as 'K V cash' etc. Speaker attribution may be slightly off for short interjections.
